before.label: Roland Barthes
before.description: Extends analysis of signs to everyday cultural meanings and myths; later work challenges stable authorship and readings. His trajectory crosses a simple structuralist/poststructuralist division.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Mythologies (1957); “The Death of the Author” (1967); S/Z (1970).

after.label: Roland Barthes
after.description: Analyzes myth as the naturalization of historically produced meanings and studies how historical narratives signify reality. His challenge to authorial closure shifts attention to textual plurality and the reader. Historians and cultural theorists adapt these arguments while disputing their scope.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Mythologies (1957); “The Death of the Author” (1967); S/Z (1970).
after.scope_note: Individual thinker with a changing trajectory, not one fixed structuralist method. Mythologies (1957), Elements of Semiology (1964), the history/authorship essays (1967), The Reality Effect (1968) and S/Z (1970) are distinct works. Saussure, Jakobson, Kristeva, Nietzsche, Marx and Vernant are named resources with different scopes. Bann questions the implied decline of historians’ concern with reality; Hebdige makes a particular style-analysis adaptation. Rhetorical effects do not alone establish that events are imaginary, and the theoretical reader is not a biography of actual readers. S/Z and later photographic inquiry await bounded primary reading; the clinical analogies and sweeping historical generalizations remain attributed.

before.label: Friedrich Nietzsche
before.description: Questions apparently timeless moral categories by investigating their contingent emergence. An important resource for Foucault’s genealogical approach.
before.representative_figures_and_works: On the Genealogy of Morality (1887); Foucault’s “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971).

after.label: Friedrich Nietzsche
after.description: Questions the historical formation and value of moral judgments. Genealogy distinguishes the emergence of a practice from its changing uses; perspectival knowledge requires active interpretation. His earlier essay examines the benefits and dangers of monumental, antiquarian and critical uses of the past.
after.representative_figures_and_works: On the Genealogy of Morality (1887); Foucault’s “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971).
after.scope_note: Individual philosophical precursor, not simply an anticipation of Foucault. The 1874 history essay and 1887 Genealogy pose distinct questions. Rée and Schopenhauer are explicit interlocutors; Burckhardt supplies a named cultural-historical example. Documentary inquiry and disciplined plurality complicate a blanket relativist reading. Foucault and Barthes appropriate different aspects. Nietzsche’s hierarchical, gendered, religious and physiological generalizations remain situated arguments, not verified historical facts. Original German, cited interlocutors and the witness behind Barthes’s aphorism remain bounded limits.
